Description: ask the patient necessary ice-breaking questions (such as what's the purpose of the visit or any necessary question to make the patient feel comfortable and build connections; these are not related to the symptoms and it is only for ice-breaking) to initiate the interview. the criteria are met when the patient has an elevated or expansive mood
Patient_Story: I have elevated mood. I feel like I am on top of the world. I have been feeling incredibly euphoric, as if I could accomplish anything. I remember staying up late talking with friends, planning an elaborate trip that I impulsively decided we should take, and I even booked the hotel without thinking twice about the cost. However, it all came crashing down when I suddenly felt depressed and withdrawn, barely able to get out of bed for a few days afterward. The stark contrast between those highs and lows has left me feeling a bit confused and concerned about what’s happening to me.

Description: Determine if the patient's elevated or expansive mood is primarily due to the physiological effects of a substance, such as drugs, alcohol, or medications for any medical conditions. The criteria is met when the patient's mood disturbance is directly linked to the substance's effects.
Patient_Story: Lately, I’ve felt a genuine sense of joy and enthusiasm that doesn’t seem tied to any substances. For instance, when I made the decision to adopt a rescue dog named Max, my mood soared. I spent hours playing with him at the park, feeling a natural high from just being outside and watching him frolic, completely free of any alcohol or drugs.

Description: Determine if the patient's elevated or expansive mood is primarily caused by the physiological effects of a general medical condition, such as physical health issues. This assessment should focus on whether the mood disturbance is directly linked to the underlying medical condition.
Patient_Story: I’ve been feeling really great lately, especially since I started a new job that I love. There’s been no physical health issues affecting my mood—just genuine excitement and joy that comes from pursuing my passions. For example, last weekend, I spent time at a local art fair, soaking in the creativity around me, which only added to my happiness.

Description: the patient has reported clinically significant manic. criteria met for a manic episode (i.e., **at least 1 week of elevated**, expansive or irritable mood accompanied by increased activity or energy and other characteristic symptoms sufficiently severe to cause marked impairment). Duration has to be explicitly asked.
Patient_Story: I've been feeling really good recently, and yes, I've had moments of elevated mood, but they haven't lasted for more than a few days at a time. Like last week, I was on a high after finishing a big project at work, and I spent the entire Saturday painting with friends until sunset, but it was just that one day. I often feel excited about things, but I wouldn’t say it’s been any serious, ongoing manic episode.

Description: The patient has reported hypomanic and at least one Major Depressive Epsidoe. Criteria met for a hypomanic episode (i.e., at least 4 days of elevated, expansive, or irritable mood accompanied by increased activity or energy and other characteristic symptoms not severe enough to cause marked impairment) and has at other times met criteria for a Major Depression Episode.  Duration has to be explicitly asked.
Patient_Story: I've had a few days here and there where I felt particularly energetic and enthusiastic, like when I organized a surprise birthday party for my sister last month. I was buzzing with ideas and arrangements, and it felt great to channel my creativity. However, those moments were short-lived, and I can’t recall ever feeling consistently high or low enough to meet any serious criteria for a hypomanic or major depressive episode.

Description: The criteria are met if the patient explicitly reported at least 2 years of hypomanic symptoms along with periods of depressed mood. Duration should be explicitly asked.
Patient_Story: I’ve experienced some ups and downs, but I wouldn't say they lasted long enough to be serious. Like, last summer, I was really energized for a couple of weeks as I was planning a trip with friends to the mountains, and I was super excited about it. However, once the trip was over, my mood returned to normal, and I certainly haven’t felt depressed for any extended period—to be honest, it’s just been those brief bursts of excitement here and there.

Description: The criteria is met if elevated or euphoric mood confined to periods of gambling
Patient_Story: I’ve recently found this incredible rush whenever I engage in online gambling, particularly on poker sites. There was a night last week when I won a few hundred dollars, and I felt elated—like I was on top of the world. My friends even noticed how animated I was, telling stories about my big win and all the plans I had for my winnings. It was an intense high, but it seemed to only arise during those gambling sessions, and once I stepped away from the screen, my mood would settle back down.

Description: The criteria are met if the persistent and problematic gambling behaviour leads to clinically significant impairment or distress. This means the symptoms should be significant enough to cause notable distress or impairment, making them a central concern in the patient's overall condition.
Patient_Story: While I do enjoy playing poker online, it’s more of a fun hobby for me rather than something that causes distress. Just last weekend, I spent a few hours playing with friends, and while I got a bit excited when I won a hand, I wasn’t overly invested in the outcomes. I can easily walk away and focus on other things in my life, like my painting or spending time with Max, without feeling any significant impact on my day-to-day mood or responsibilities.

Description: Normal Gambling Behavior

We laughed and joked while playing, and although I won a few hands, I never felt the urge to chase losses or spend more than I intended. It was just a light-hearted way to enjoy some time together, and afterward, I went home feeling happy but not obsessed with the game or its outcomes.

Description: Evaluate if the elevated or expansive mood reported by the patient is the primary focus of the clinical picture and is of sufficient severity to require clinical attention.
